claim: Domain vocabulary mismatch can increase token counts by fragmenting frequent in-domain terms.
source_citation: Herold et al. 2025; Liyanage & Yvon 2026; Dagan et al. 2024
how_we_test_or_bound_it: Measure total tokens, tokens/byte, and tokens/word on held-out Azure docs for general vs domain tokenizers; report by document stratum.

claim: BPE subword vocabularies are corpus-frequency dependent and can handle rare words with fixed vocabularies.
relevance_to_us: Justifies training BPE on Azure docs and comparing compression.
how_we_test_or_bound_it: Train matched-vocabulary BPE tokenizers on domain corpus and compare with general byte-level BPE; do not claim MT-quality effects.

claim: Byte-level BPE is robust for arbitrary text but not necessarily optimal for specialized compression.
source_citation: Radford et al. 2019; OpenAI tiktoken README
relevance_to_us: Azure docs include code, IDs, URLs, and arbitrary symbols.
how_we_test_or_bound_it: Use byte-level BPE/tiktoken as robust baseline; quantify whether domain tokenizer reduces tokens without losing reversibility/coverage.

claim: Unigram/SentencePiece tokenizers can train directly from raw sentences and avoid whitespace pretokenization assumptions.
relevance_to_us: Azure docs mix prose, markdown, code, and non-word delimiters.
how_we_test_or_bound_it: If included, hold normalization and corpus constant; compare raw-text handling and compression to BPE baselines.

claim: Fertility and parity are useful intrinsic metrics but are not always predictive of downstream LLM performance.
how_we_test_or_bound_it: Report compression/runtime only; explicitly state no downstream quality claim unless model evaluation is added.

claim: Tokenizer length disparities can affect user-facing cost, latency, and effective context size.
relevance_to_us: Token-count reductions may matter operationally for prompt budgets.
how_we_test_or_bound_it: Translate token reductions into context-budget deltas; avoid claiming actual LLM latency unless measured.

claim: Specialized tokenizers can improve downstream performance when tokenizer and pretraining data are controlled.
relevance_to_us: Motivates interest, but our study is intrinsic.
how_we_test_or_bound_it: Do not claim downstream improvement; cite as motivation and boundary.

claim: Domain adaptation can improve models even without changing the tokenizer.
how_we_test_or_bound_it: State that tokenizer specialization is one lever; our design does not compare against domain-adaptive pretraining.

claim: Pre-tokenization regex, tokenizer size, and tokenizer training data can affect speed, memory, context, and performance.
relevance_to_us: Our CPU study could be confounded by implementation and pretokenization choices.
how_we_test_or_bound_it: Record regex/normalization settings; run matched-vocab experiments; separate encode throughput from token count.

claim: Vocabulary augmentation can be designed to never increase token counts relative to a base tokenizer.
relevance_to_us: Useful if project implements add-token adaptation rather than train-from-scratch.
how_we_test_or_bound_it: If augmenting, verify per-document token_count(adapted) <= token_count(base); otherwise mark out of scope.

claim: Fixed-size token replacement can improve domain compression without increasing vocabulary size.
relevance_to_us: Closest to controlled fixed-vocab Azure tokenizer specialization.
how_we_test_or_bound_it: Run same-vocab-size domain tokenizer/adaptation and compare against general baseline; bootstrap document-level reductions.

claim: Vocabulary adaptation plus model adaptation may reduce training time or parameter growth.
relevance_to_us: Interesting but outside CPU-only tokenizer efficiency unless LLM adaptation is added.
how_we_test_or_bound_it: Boundary claim only; do not mention training-time/parameter benefits as our expected outcome.

claim: Domain-specific token inventory examples are explanatory, not sufficient evidence.
relevance_to_us: Azure terms may look compelling anecdotally.
how_we_test_or_bound_it: Use examples only after quantitative held-out metrics and confidence intervals.
